concepts.name: Abhaya Mudra: Meaning, Occurrence, and Cross-Traditional Usage
key_dimensions: Gesture of protection/fearlessness — raised right hand, palm outward
Shared usage across Buddhist, Hindu (Vishnu, Shiva), and Jain iconography — trap: not exclusive to Buddhism
Regional variations: Gandhara vs. Mathura vs. South Indian sculptural rendering
Association with specific narratives — e.g., Buddha's gesture after Enlightenment or during the Nalagiri elephant episode

concepts.name: Varada Mudra: Gift-Giving Gesture and Iconographic Pairing
key_dimensions: Downward extended right hand with open palm — gesture of boon-granting
Often paired with Abhaya Mudra (right-left combination) in standing Buddhist and Hindu images
Appears on Bodhisattvas, Vishnu, and goddess figures — distinction in which hand is used
Trap: Confused with Vitarka Mudra — difference lies in finger position (open palm vs. raised index finger)

concepts.name: Dhyana Mudra: Meditation Gesture and Buddhist Iconographic Significance
key_dimensions: Both hands resting in lap, right over left, thumbs touching — gesture of meditation
Exclusively associated with seated Buddha images and Dhyani Buddhas (Amitabha especially)
Key iconographic marker distinguishing meditating Buddha from teaching Buddha (Dharmachakra Mudra)
Presence in Vajrayana iconography — held vessel (begging bowl) as additional attribute in some traditions

concepts.name: Dharmachakra Mudra: The Teaching Gesture and Its Narrative Context
key_dimensions: Both hands raised at chest level, fingers forming a wheel gesture — symbolizes the First Sermon at Sarnath
Iconographic marker for the 'Dharmachakrapravartana' — First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma
Key example: Sarnath Buddha (Gupta period, 5th century CE) — considered finest rendering
Trap: Distinguish from Vitarka Mudra — both involve raised hands but differ in number of hands and symbolic context

concepts.name: Bhumisparsha Mudra: Earth-Witness Gesture and the Maravijaya Narrative
key_dimensions: Right hand touching the ground, left hand in lap — calls earth to witness the Buddha's enlightenment
Directly linked to the 'Maravijaya' (victory over Mara) narrative at Bodh Gaya
Most prevalent mudra in Southeast Asian Buddhist sculpture (Thailand, Cambodia, Myanmar)
Trap: Sometimes confused with Varada Mudra — key distinction is the downward reach touching the ground vs. open palm gesture

concepts.name: Vitarka Mudra: Gesture of Discussion and Doctrinal Debate
key_dimensions: Hand raised with index finger and thumb touching, other fingers extended — gesture of argument/teaching
Used for both Buddha and Bodhisattvas; also appears in Hindu iconography for teacher figures
Tarjani Mudra (raised index finger alone — gesture of warning) is a common confusion trap
In Vajrayana: when both hands perform Vitarka, it is called 'Vyakhyana Mudra'

concepts.name: Attributes (Ayudhas) of Vishnu: The Panchaayudha and Iconographic Identification
key_dimensions: Four canonical attributes: Shankha (conch), Chakra (discus), Gada (mace), Padma (lotus) — held in four hands
Specific hand-attribute assignment varies by school: Vaikhanasa vs. Pancharatra Agama traditions
Trap: The Shrivatsa mark on chest and Kaustubha gem are body marks, not held attributes — frequently confused
Identification of Vishnu forms (Trivikrama, Vaikunta, Chaturbhuja) based on attribute combinations and poses

concepts.name: Nataraja Iconography: Cosmic Dance and Symbolic Attributes
key_dimensions: Four arms: upper right holds damaru (drum — creation), upper left holds agni (fire — destruction), lower right shows Abhaya Mudra, lower left points to raised foot (Gajahasta)
Dwarf Apasmara Purusha beneath foot — symbol of ignorance/ego being crushed
Prabhavali (ring of fire/flames) — represents the cosmic cycle of Samsara
Trap: Chidambaram's Nataraja is the canonical form but regional variations (e.g., Ellora, Badami) show slight differences — UPSC may test specific attributes

concepts.name: Mahishasuramardini Iconography: Multi-Armed Durga and Battle Attributes
key_dimensions: Standard form: 8 or 10 arms carrying weapons borrowed from various gods — Trishula (Shiva), Chakra (Vishnu), Bow (Vayu), etc.
Lion (Simha) as vahana — distinguishes Durga from other goddess forms
Pallava Mahabalipuram rock-cut panel vs. Gupta period renderings — stylistic comparison
Trap: Chamunda (another fierce goddess) also slays demons but has distinct emaciated iconography — not to be confused with Mahishasuramardini

concepts.name: Ganesha Iconography: Essential Attributes and Regional Variations
key_dimensions: Standard attributes: broken tusk (right), modaka (sweet) in lower right or trunk-tip, axe (parashu), noose (pasha) — four-armed canonical form
Vahana: Mushaka (mouse/rat) — symbolic of Ganesha controlling desires/ego
Trap: Direction of trunk curl — trunk curving left (Vamamukhi) considered auspicious for home worship; right-curving (Dakshinamukhi) considered more powerful but strict ritual rules apply
Heramba Ganapati (five-headed, lion vahana) vs. standard Ganapati — a higher-difficulty distinction

concepts.name: Shiva Linga Iconography: Typology and Textual Classification
key_dimensions: Three-part structure: Brahma-bhaga (square base), Vishnu-bhaga (octagonal middle), Shiva-bhaga (cylindrical top)
Classification: Svayambhu (self-manifested), Daivika (made by gods), Manava (man-made) — from Agamic texts
Mukhalinga (face carved on shaft) — e.g., Ekamukha, Chaturmukha — bridges linga and anthropomorphic iconography
Trap: The Yoni-pitha (base receptacle) is iconographically significant and represents Shakti — UPSC may test the combined symbolism

concepts.name: Bodhisattva Iconography: Distinguishing Avalokiteshvara, Manjushri, and Maitreya
key_dimensions: Avalokiteshvara: Lotus (padma) in hand, Amitabha Buddha in crown, associated with compassion — Padmapani form most common
Manjushri: Sword (Khadga) in right hand cutting ignorance, book (Prajnaparamita) in left — deity of wisdom
Maitreya: Stupa in crown (future Buddha), water vessel (kamandalu), associated with Tushita heaven
Trap: Vajrapani (thunderbolt holder) is often grouped with Avalokiteshvara and Manjushri as the trinity of Bodhisattvas — specific attributes must be memorized

concepts.name: Tribhanga Posture: Aesthetic Convention and Iconographic Significance
key_dimensions: Triple-flexed pose: neck, torso, and knee bent in opposite directions — S-curve body posture
Primarily associated with Krishna, female deities (Apsaras), and dancing figures in Indian sculpture
Distinguished from Samabhanga (equal/symmetric pose — associated with Vishnu standing) and Atibhanga (extreme bend — associated with sensuous female figures)
Trap: Samapada (feet together, strictly frontal — common in early Buddhist art) vs. Tribhanga — UPSC may test the stylistic evolution

concepts.name: Lakshmi Iconography: Gajalakshmi Form and Attribute Symbolism
key_dimensions: Gajalakshmi: Two elephants flanking and anointing goddess — fertility, sovereignty, and abundance symbolism
Attributes: Lotus (padma) in both upper hands, lower hands in Varada and Abhaya Mudras — gold coins sometimes shown
Association with Vishnu: Lakshmi as consort — Vaikuntha panels show Lakshmi at Vishnu's feet or beside him
Trap: Gajalakshmi motif predates formal Vaishnavism — appears on Sanchi Stupa (Buddhist context) and Mauryan coins — cross-religious usage is a key UPSC trap

concepts.name: Saraswati Iconography: Attributes of Learning and Arts
key_dimensions: Standard attributes: Veena (lute — music), Pustaka (book — learning), Akshamala (rosary — time/meditation), Kamandalu (water pot)
Vahana: Hamsa (swan or goose) — symbol of discrimination between real and unreal (Viveka)
Trap: Some forms show Saraswati with Chakra and Shankha in additional hands — this is a Vaishnava Saraswati form, distinct from standard iconography
Early Buddhist Saraswati images (e.g., at Mathura) show her with a simpler iconography — evolution of attributes over time

concepts.name: Ardhanarisvara Iconography: Composite Form and Symbolic Dimensions
key_dimensions: Right half: Shiva (third eye, matted hair, Trishula, tiger skin); Left half: Parvati (crown, jewelry, sari, lotus or mirror)
Symbolizes the inseparability of Purusha (cosmic male) and Prakriti (cosmic female) principles
Earliest examples: Kushana period; finest: Elephanta Cave and Badami Cave panels
Trap: The vahana Nandi appears on the Shiva half — and in some panels a lotus or peacock appears on the Parvati half; the division of attributes is a frequent question source

concepts.name: Karanas and Hasta Mudras in Classical Dance Iconography (Natyashastra Context)
key_dimensions: Natyashastra describes 108 karanas (combined hand + body poses) — many codified in temple sculpture (e.g., Chidambaram has 108 karana panels)
Asamyuta Hastas (single hand gestures — 28 types) vs. Samyuta Hastas (combined hand gestures — 24 types) in classical dance
Nataraja sculpture directly embodies karana iconography — 'Urdhva Tandava' karana is the raised-leg form
Trap: UPSC may conflate mudras in worship context (ritual Tantric mudras) with mudras in sculptural/dance iconography — they are related but distinct systems

concepts.name: Attributes of Surya (Sun God): Iconographic Distinctives and Regional Forms
key_dimensions: Standard attributes: Two lotus flowers held in both hands, crown (Kirita Mukuta), high boots (Udaka) — boots are a unique marker distinguishing Surya from other deities
Two attendants: Danda (holding a staff) and Pingala (holding a book) flank Surya; archer Vivasvan form has bow
Konark Sun Temple: Chariot with 7 horses (days of week), 12 wheels (months) — iconographic program as cosmological allegory
Trap: High boots on Surya are considered a Central Asian (Scythian/Kushan) iconographic influence — an important art-history connection UPSC has tested

concepts.name: Panchamukha (Five-Headed) Shiva: Sadashiva Form and Theological Mapping
key_dimensions: Five faces: Tatpurusha (east — grace), Aghora (south — fierce), Vamadeva (north — benevolent), Sadyojata (west — creation), Ishana (upward — omniscience)
Elephanta Cave's Trimurti (Maheshmurti) panel — three visible faces from Sadashiva iconography — considered finest rock-cut sculpture
Each face associated with one of the five functions: Creation, Preservation, Destruction, Concealment, Grace (Panchakritya)
Trap: Elephanta's Trimurti is NOT a Trimurti of Brahma-Vishnu-Shiva but three aspects of Shiva alone — a classic UPSC misconception trap

concepts.name: Yaksha and Yakshi Iconography: Fertility Symbolism and Buddhist-Hindu Overlap
key_dimensions: Yakshi (female): Salabhanjika pose — woman grasping a tree branch (associated with fertility and abundance); prominent at Sanchi, Mathura, Didarganj
Attributes: Full figure, elaborate jewelry, absence of divine attributes — distinguished from goddess figures by context and lack of mudras
Didarganj Yakshi (Mauryan period): Chauri-bearer (fly-whisk holder) — iconic polished Mauryan surface technique

Trap: Yaksha/Yakshi are nature spirits absorbed into both Buddhist and Hindu iconographic programs — their appearance at Buddhist sites (Sanchi torana) does NOT make them Buddhist deities; UPSC tests this contextual distinction
